Introducing FIMS input data

Source: vignettes/fims-input-data.Rmd
fims-input-data.Rmd

Other sources of information

This vignette is an expansion of the “Data” section in the FIMS overview vignette. It provides more details about the data structure needed for a FIMS model and how to prepare your data for use in a FIMS model using the FIMSFrame() function.

The FIMS cheatsheet includes a quick summary of the input data format.

The help page for the FIMS::data_big data set (https://noaa-fims.github.io/FIMS/reference/data_big.html or via ?FIMS::data_big) provides detailed information about the input data format.

Note: this vignette does not include anything about model configuration, which is covered in the overview vignette linked above.

Data format

The input data for a FIMS model is a single long data frame with the following columns: type, fleet, age, length, timing, observed, unit, and uncertainty. Both the single table and long format are in contrast to the input format for some legacy stock assessment models where the data are provided in multiple tables, each with a different format. The SS3 data file, for instance, has separate tables for catch, indices, age compositions, length compositions, with wide tables for the composition data (each age or length bin has a different column). The use of a single, long table for data input used by FIMS makes it easier to summarize and filter the data across data types (e.g., by fleet, timing, age, etc.), as well as being better suited to the widely-used tidyverse collection of packages in R.

Two drawbacks of the long format are (1) some information is duplicated, and (2) the long format is harder to read and understand by looking at the raw data frame. To meet this second challenge, the FIMS team is working on functions to summarize, visualize, and check for errors in the input data.

The currently available values for the type column are “age_comp”, “age_to_length_conversion”, “ageing_error”, “index”, “catch”, “length_bin”, “length_comp”, and “weight_at_age”. The “weight_at_age”, “ageing_error”, and “age_to_length_conversion” types are not currently treated as data in the sense that they are not included in the likelihood. They are used in the population dynamics calculations or, for “ageing_error”, in the expected age compositions.

The individual data types are described in more detail below after introducing the example data set that is included in the package.

data_big

A sample data frame for a catch-at-age model with both ages and lengths is stored in the package as data_big. This data set is based on data that was used in Li et al. (2021) for the Model Comparison Project (github site). The length data have since been added data-raw/data_big.R based on an age–length conversion matrix. To see how this example data frame was created, see the R script here R/data_big.R.

FIMSFrame()

FIMSFrame() must be used to create a data object that can be passed to a FIMS model. This function returns an object that has the FIMSFrame class. This class contains a data slot that stores the input data frame and several other slots that store summary information about the object, e.g., the fleet names, the number of age bins, etc. All of this information can be accessed using get_*() functions, e.g., get_n_years(), get_fleets(). Every fleet named in the data must have catch, index, or composition data. FIMSFrame() returns an error otherwise, so a misspelled fleet name in other rows does not add a fleet to the model.

When you execute FIMSFrame() on a long data frame, such as data_big, the function executes several error checks to help ensure that your data is ready for a FIMS model. For example, until the internal estimation of growth is possible, all catch-at-age models require weight-at-age data. If your data frame does not have weight-at-age data, then FIMSFrame() will error and return helpful information on what you are missing.

The output of FIMSFrame() also contains summary information about your data and has an internal plotting function. See the FIMS overview vignette for more information.

data_4_model <- FIMSFrame(data_big)
data_4_model

Catch (type == "catch")

The catch data type contains the total catch in weight or numbers for each time step. FIMS does not yet include the option to model discards internally, so “catch” should account for all catch. The catch are not associated with an age or length so those columns should only contain NA values. The unit column should be mt for catch in weight or number for catch in numbers, and all catch rows of a fleet must use the same unit. FIMS fits mt catch to the expected catch in weight and number catch to the expected catch in numbers. FIMS does not rescale catch, so catch in numbers must be on the same scale as numbers at age in the model. For example, when weight at age is in mt per fish, catch in numbers is the number of fish, not thousands of fish. The uncertainty column should be the standard deviation of the logged observations if you are using the lognormal distribution to fit your data. log_Fmort parameters for each fleet and time step with catch can be estimated to fit the model to the catch data, informed by the uncertainty values. Common practice is to set the uncertainty to a small number, like 0.001, so the catch data are fit closely. A catch of 0 means the fleet did not fish in that time step. setup_default_parameters() fixes log_Fmort for that fleet and year at -200, so fishing mortality is effectively 0, and the 0 is left out of the likelihood. It is reported as -999 in the output, the same as missing data. If you estimate log_Fmort in that year instead, initialize_fims() warns, because nothing in the data informs it. A fleet with a catch of 0 in every year and no composition data gives no information on its selectivity. Use -999, not 0, for a missing catch.

# first three rows of the catch data
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "catch") |>
  head(3)
##    type  fleet age length timing observed unit
## 1 catch fleet1  NA     NA      1 161.6455   mt
## 2 catch fleet1  NA     NA      2 461.0895   mt
## 3 catch fleet1  NA     NA      3 747.2900   mt
##                                                             uncertainty
## 1 ~ dlnorm(meanlog = log_catch_expected, sdlog =  0.00999975001354021 )
## 2 ~ dlnorm(meanlog = log_catch_expected, sdlog =  0.00999975001354021 )
## 3 ~ dlnorm(meanlog = log_catch_expected, sdlog =  0.00999975001354021 )
# time series plot of catch data
library(ggplot2)
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "catch") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = timing, y = observed)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  ggtitle("Catch time series in data_big example data set")

Indices (type == "index")

The index data type contains the relative or absolute abundance index for each time step. The inputs are similar to catch, in having NA values for age and length, mt or number for unit (1 unit for all index rows of a fleet), and index uncertainty as the standard deviation of the logged observations. An index of 0 or less cannot be fit with the lognormal distribution, and FIMSFrame() returns an error for it. Use -999 for a missing index, or a distribution that allows 0.

# first three rows of the index data
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "index") |>
  head(3)
##    type   fleet age length timing    observed unit
## 1 index survey1  NA     NA      1 0.006117418   mt
## 2 index survey1  NA     NA      2 0.007156588   mt
## 3 index survey1  NA     NA      3 0.006553376   mt
##                                                           uncertainty
## 1 ~ dlnorm(meanlog = log_index_expected, sdlog =  0.198042200435365 )
## 2 ~ dlnorm(meanlog = log_index_expected, sdlog =  0.198042200435365 )
## 3 ~ dlnorm(meanlog = log_index_expected, sdlog =  0.198042200435365 )
# time series plot of index data
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "index") |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = timing, y = observed)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::geom_pointrange(ggplot2::aes(
    ymin = stats::qlnorm(
      p = 0.025,
      meanlog = log(observed),
      sdlog = unlist(
        FIMS:::parse_data_distribution(uncertainty)$sdlog,
        use.names = FALSE
      )
    ),
    ymax = stats::qlnorm(
      p = 0.975,
      meanlog = log(observed),
      sdlog = unlist(
        FIMS:::parse_data_distribution(uncertainty)$sdlog,
        use.names = FALSE
      )
    )
  )) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  ggplot2::ggtitle("Index time series in data_big example data set")

Age compositions (type == "age_comp")

The age-composition data type contains the age distribution of a fleet for a time step. The age column contains integer ages defining the age bins. While standard FIMS models typically assume age bins start at zero, the data_big example currently uses ages ranging from 1–12, and thus, recruitment will be age-1 fish not age-0 fish. The observed column contains either the number or the proportion of the catch or survey in each age bin. The unit column should be either “number” or “proportion”. If “proportion” is used, the observations are checked at a later step to confirm that they sum to 1.0. The uncertainty column should be the input sample size for the time step (equal across all ages within that time step). When the unit is set to a proportion, the sample size is multiplied by the proportion; however, when it is set to a number, the sample size is ignored.

# first three rows of the age composition data
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "age_comp") |>
  head(3)
##       type  fleet age length timing observed       unit
## 1 age_comp fleet1   1     NA      1    0.070 proportion
## 2 age_comp fleet1   2     NA      1    0.100 proportion
## 3 age_comp fleet1   3     NA      1    0.115 proportion
##                                            uncertainty
## 1 ~ dmultinom(prob = agecomp_proportion, size =  200 )
## 2 ~ dmultinom(prob = agecomp_proportion, size =  200 )
## 3 ~ dmultinom(prob = agecomp_proportion, size =  200 )
# plot of age compositions by time step
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "age_comp") |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    ggplot2::aes(x = age, y = observed)
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  ggplot2::xlab("Age") +
  ggplot2::ylab("Number") +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~timing) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = get_ages(data_4_model)) +
  ggtitle("Age compositions by time step in data_big example data set")

Length compositions (type == "length_comp")

The length-composition data are similar to the age compositions, except with values in the length column and age = NA. The length column identifies the length bin for each observation by its lower edge. A bin holds lengths from its lower edge up to the next lower edge. For example, with length values of 0, 50, …, 1100, the bin labeled 250 includes fish measuring at least 250 mm but less than 300 mm (250–299 mm for whole-number measurements). The next bin, labeled 300, includes fish measuring at least 300 mm but less than 350 mm (i.e. [300, 350) in interval notation). When growth is estimated in FIMS, the first bin also holds all smaller fish and the last bin holds all larger fish. With fixed age_to_length_conversion rows, those rows set what each bin holds. The observed column contains either the number or the proportion of fish in each length bin. The unit column should be either “number” or “proportion”. The uncertainty column should be the input sample size for the time step, repeated across all length bins in that time step. When the unit is set to a proportion, the sample size is multiplied by the proportion; however, when it is set to a number, the sample size is ignored.

When length compositions are included, FIMS needs a way to convert numbers at age into numbers at length. This can come from fixed age_to_length_conversion rows or from a growth-derived age-to-length conversion using the VonB-Schnute Growth module.

# first three rows of the length composition data
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "length_comp") |>
  head(3)
##          type  fleet age length timing     observed       unit
## 1 length_comp fleet1  NA      0      1 9.238773e-18 proportion
## 2 length_comp fleet1  NA     50      1 5.892510e-12 proportion
## 3 length_comp fleet1  NA    100      1 1.610390e-07 proportion
##                                               uncertainty
## 1 ~ dmultinom(prob = lengthcomp_proportion, size =  200 )
## 2 ~ dmultinom(prob = lengthcomp_proportion, size =  200 )
## 3 ~ dmultinom(prob = lengthcomp_proportion, size =  200 )
# plot of length compositions by time step
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "length_comp") |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    ggplot2::aes(x = length, y = observed)
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  ggplot2::xlab("Length") +
  ggplot2::ylab("Number") +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~timing) +
  ggtitle("Length compositions by time step in data_big example data set")

Length bins (type == "length_bin")

The length_bin data type defines length bins without providing length-composition observations. These rows are useful when a model needs length-bin geometry for a growth-derived age-to-length conversion, but the user is not fitting length-composition data for that fleet.

For length_bin rows, the length column contains the lower edge of each length bin, the same as for length compositions. The observed, age, and uncertainty columns should usually be NA. The fleet column identifies which fleet or survey the length bins apply to, and timing can be NA unless fleet-specific timing is needed.

length_bin rows with fleet = NA and timing = NA set the population length bins. These bins are for the whole population and do not set bins for any fleet. This differs from age_to_length_conversion rows, where fleet = NA means the conversion is shared by all fleets.

Growth uses the population bins for the distribution of length at each age. FIMS then maps that distribution onto each fleet’s bins to get the expected length composition for that fleet. The population bins must cover every fleet’s bins, and no population bin can be wider than a fleet bin it overlaps.

For example, suppose a fleet has bins of 0 to 50 mm and 50 to 100 mm. Population bins of 0 to 25, 25 to 50, 50 to 75, and 75 to 100 mm meet these rules, and the fleet edge at 50 mm is also a population edge. A different set of population bins with a bin of 40 to 60 mm would cross that edge. FIMS splits the fish in that bin between the 2 fleet bins by how much of the bin falls in each, as if fish were spread evenly within the bin. Here half go to each fleet bin. Making every fleet bin edge a population bin edge avoids this split.

The length values are the lower edges of the bins. The first bin also holds all fish shorter than the first lower edge. The last bin is open-ended and holds all fish at or above the last lower edge. FIMS gives the last bin the same width as the bin before it, which sets the length used for its weight. Set the last lower edge high enough that few fish fall in this bin. FIMS writes a warning to the log (see get_log_warnings()) when more than 1% of the fish at an age in a year are in it.

Without these rows, FIMS builds population bins only when a fleet has length bins. They are 1 unit wide (1 mm for data_big) from the smallest fleet lower edge to the largest fleet upper edge, plus 1 more bin. With no population bins, weight at age is the weight at mean length. Adding these rows can change weight at age, and so biomass, even without length compositions. This is because weight at age is then averaged over the length distribution at each age. Population length bins need a growth module that gives length at age, so they are not used with EWAA growth.

# population length bins 10 mm wide with lower edges from 0 to 1190 mm, which
# span the data_big fleet length bins (0 to 1150 mm)
population_length_bins <- tibble::tibble(
  type = "length_bin",
  fleet = NA_character_,
  age = NA_integer_,
  length = seq(0, 1190, by = 10),
  timing = NA_real_,
  observed = NA_real_,
  unit = NA_character_,
  uncertainty = NA_character_
)
data_with_population_bins <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  FIMS::data_big,
  population_length_bins
)
FIMSFrame(data_with_population_bins)

Weight-at-age data (type == "weight_at_age")

The weight-at-age data are not currently included in the likelihood and are just used for converting from numbers to biomass in the population dynamics. The unit column should be mt and the uncertainty should be NA.

The population weight at age has fleet = NA. It is used for biomass and spawning biomass, and for the catch and index weight of any fleet without its own weight at age. Rows with a fleet name are that fleet’s weight at age for its catch and index weight, for example from port samples or survey samples. For each year, a fleet uses its own rows for that year, then its own timing = NA rows, then the population weight at age, so a fleet only needs rows for the years that differ. If there are no fleet = NA rows and only 1 fleet has weight rows, those rows are used as the population weight at age, with a warning.

Rows with timing = NA are the default for every year, and rows with a timing replace that default for that year only. Timings outside the model years and the year after the last are an error. Every timing that is used needs 1 row for each model age, and rows are never averaged. Without timing = NA rows, every model year needs its own rows, plus the year after the last model year, because FIMS reports spawning biomass at the beginning of the year for every year, including the year after the last catches are removed from the population.

The weight-at-age observations for the data_big are identical across time steps and are provided for timing = 1 to 31 with fleet = NA. The same weights could be given as 1 set of rows with timing = NA.

Ageing error (type == "ageing_error")

Ageing error data are optional. Age readers do not always assign the true age, which spreads a strong year class across neighboring ages. With ageing error rows, each fleet’s expected age composition is moved from true age to observed age before it is compared to the data. Length compositions, catch, and indices still use true age, and ageing error is not part of the likelihood.

Each row gives the probability that a fish of one true age is read as one observed age. The observed age goes in age, the true age in uncertainty, and the probability in observed, with unit = "proportion". The uncertainty column holds formulas for other data types, so true ages are stored as text, e.g., uncertainty = as.character(true_age).

Each set of rows is a full matrix over the model ages, and the probabilities for each true age must sum to 1. Sums within 1e-3 of 1 are rescaled to exactly 1, with a warning, and larger differences are an error. If a matrix was rounded to fewer than 3 decimal places, first check that uncertainty holds the true age and age the observed age, then divide each true age’s probabilities by their total before adding it. Probability on observed ages below the youngest model age is added to that age, and above the oldest model age to the plus group, with a warning. Every observed age needs a total probability, summed across true ages, of at least 1e-3, because an expected proportion of 0 makes the likelihood undefined.

Every model age needs rows as a true age, in uncertainty. Rows for true ages outside the model ages are not used, with a warning. Each row is the probability of each observed age given one true age, so probabilities for observed ages within a row can be added, but combining rows for different true ages needs the number of fish at each true age, which is unknown. The model has no fish below the youngest age, e.g., true age 0 in a model that starts at age 1, so dropping those rows changes nothing. Above the plus group, the row for the plus-group true age is used for every fish in the plus group.

Ageing error can vary by fleet and year. For each fleet and year, the most specific rows are used:

  1. rows for that fleet and that timing,
  2. rows for that fleet with timing = NA,
  3. rows with fleet = NA and that timing, and
  4. rows with fleet = NA and timing = NA.

Rows with fleet = NA apply to every fleet with age-composition data. A timing applies to that year only. Without a timing = NA default, every model year needs its own rows, including projection years. A fleet with no rows that apply to it has no ageing error, which is also the default.

With ageing error, the reported agecomp_proportion and agecomp_expected are at observed age, while catch_numbers_at_age and index_numbers_at_age stay at true age.

data_big does not include ageing error. The example below adds a matrix where each age is read 1 year too young or too old with probability 0.1.

ageing_error_ages <- get_ages(data_4_model)
n_ageing_error_ages <- length(ageing_error_ages)
ageing_error_matrix <- diag(0.8, n_ageing_error_ages)
ageing_error_matrix[cbind(
  1:(n_ageing_error_ages - 1),
  2:n_ageing_error_ages
)] <- 0.1
ageing_error_matrix[cbind(
  2:n_ageing_error_ages,
  1:(n_ageing_error_ages - 1)
)] <- 0.1
ageing_error_matrix[1, 1] <- 0.9
ageing_error_matrix[n_ageing_error_ages, n_ageing_error_ages] <- 0.9
ageing_error <- tibble::tibble(
  type = "ageing_error",
  fleet = NA_character_,
  age = rep(ageing_error_ages, times = n_ageing_error_ages),
  length = NA_real_,
  timing = NA_real_,
  # Rows of the matrix are true ages, so t() lists observed ages within each
  # true age.
  observed = as.vector(t(ageing_error_matrix)),
  unit = "proportion",
  uncertainty = as.character(rep(ageing_error_ages, each = n_ageing_error_ages))
)
data_with_ageing_error <- FIMSFrame(dplyr::bind_rows(data_big, ageing_error))
get_data(data_with_ageing_error) |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "ageing_error") |>
  head(3)
## # A tibble: 3 × 8
##   type         fleet   age length timing observed unit       uncertainty
##   <chr>        <chr> <int>  <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl> <chr>      <chr>      
## 1 ageing_error <NA>      1     NA     NA      0.9 proportion 1          
## 2 ageing_error <NA>      1     NA     NA      0.1 proportion 2          
## 3 ageing_error <NA>      1     NA     NA      0   proportion 3

Stock Synthesis and the AgeingError package describe ageing error by the mean and standard deviation of observed age at each true age, from age 0 to the population maximum age. In that convention an observed age covers the year from that age to the next, so unbiased readers have a mean of true age + 0.5 (entered as -1 in Stock Synthesis), and a standard deviation of 0.001 means almost no ageing error. The probability of each observed age is the normal probability over its year. The first and last observed ages collect the tails, as FIMS does when it folds observed ages outside the model ages, so each row sums to 1. The example below uses this convention, so vectors from Stock Synthesis or the AgeingError package can be used directly.

# Rows are true ages and columns are observed ages. Here readers are unbiased
# and the standard deviation grows with age.
n_ages <- n_ageing_error_ages
mean_observed_age <- matrix(ageing_error_ages + 0.5, n_ages, n_ages)
sd_observed_age <- matrix(0.1 * ageing_error_ages, n_ages, n_ages)
observed_age <- matrix(ageing_error_ages, n_ages, n_ages, byrow = TRUE)
# The first observed age starts at -Inf and the last ends at Inf so they
# collect the tails.
lower_bound <- observed_age
lower_bound[, 1] <- -Inf
upper_bound <- observed_age + 1
upper_bound[, n_ages] <- Inf
ageing_error_matrix <-
  stats::pnorm(upper_bound, mean_observed_age, sd_observed_age) -
  stats::pnorm(lower_bound, mean_observed_age, sd_observed_age)
round(ageing_error_matrix[1:4, 1:4], 3)
##       [,1]  [,2]  [,3]  [,4]
## [1,] 1.000 0.000 0.000 0.000
## [2,] 0.006 0.988 0.006 0.000
## [3,] 0.000 0.048 0.904 0.048
## [4,] 0.000 0.000 0.106 0.789

The AgeingError package estimates ageing error from double reads and returns it as ageing_error rows. AgeingError::run() stores 1 table per reader in ageing_error_fims, and AgeingError::ageing_error_matrix_to_fims() converts any matrix with true ages as rows. Bind the table for 1 reader, not ageing_error_fims itself, which holds every reader. The tables use fleet = NA and timing = NA, so to use different readers for different fleets or years, set fleet or timing in each table first. The tables start at true age 0 and run to the oldest age read, so FIMS drops true ages outside the model ages and adds observed ages outside them to the end ages, with warnings.

# out is the result of AgeingError::run() on double-read data.
reader1 <- out[["output"]][["ageing_error_fims"]][["reader1"]]
reader2 <- out[["output"]][["ageing_error_fims"]][["reader2"]] |>
  dplyr::mutate(fleet = "survey1")
data_with_ageing_error <- FIMSFrame(
  dplyr::bind_rows(data_big, reader1, reader2)
)

Age-to-length conversion (type == "age_to_length_conversion")

The age-to-length conversion data describe how individuals at each age are distributed across length bins. In this table, the age and length columns define every age-length bin combination, and the observed column gives the proportion (unit = "proportion") or count (unit = "number") of individuals at that age in each length bin. For each age, FIMS rescales the observed values so they sum to 1, and it warns when proportion inputs do not already sum to 1.

These data can be shared across fleets and years, or specified individually. Rows with fleet = NA are treated as shared across fleets that do not have fleet-specific information, while rows with timing = NA are treated as defaults across years that do not have their own timing. For a given fleet and year, FIMS uses rows in this order: (1) that fleet and year, (2) that fleet with timing = NA, (3) shared rows with fleet = NA for that year, and (4) shared rows with both fleet = NA and timing = NA. Each fleet-timing-age-length combination must appear at most once.

Age-to-length conversion data are not part of the likelihood. Instead, they are used in the population dynamics calculations to convert numbers at age to numbers at length when length-composition data are included and growth is not estimated internally.

Note: purely age-based models which have no length-composition data can omit the age-to-length conversion data as well.

# first and last entries in the age-to-length conversion data type
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "age_to_length_conversion") |>
  head(3)
##                       type fleet age length timing     observed       unit
## 1 age_to_length_conversion  <NA>   1      0     NA 1.261739e-16 proportion
## 2 age_to_length_conversion  <NA>   1     50     NA 8.385820e-11 proportion
## 3 age_to_length_conversion  <NA>   1    100     NA 2.297363e-06 proportion
##   uncertainty
## 1        <NA>
## 2        <NA>
## 3        <NA>
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "age_to_length_conversion") |>
  tail(3)
##                         type fleet age length timing     observed       unit
## 274 age_to_length_conversion  <NA>  12   1000     NA 8.704578e-05 proportion
## 275 age_to_length_conversion  <NA>  12   1050     NA 4.607774e-06 proportion
## 276 age_to_length_conversion  <NA>  12   1100     NA 1.572035e-07 proportion
##     uncertainty
## 274        <NA>
## 275        <NA>
## 276        <NA>
# show that the number of rows in the age-to-length conversion data type is equal to the product of the number of unique combinations of age and length
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "age_to_length_conversion") |>
  nrow()
## [1] 276
# 12 ages, 23 length bins:
length(unique(na.omit(FIMS::data_big$age))) * length(unique(na.omit(FIMS::data_big$length)))
## [1] 276
# plot of age-to-length conversion observations for the data_big example data set
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "age_to_length_conversion") |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    ggplot2::aes(
      x = age,
      y = length,
      size = observed
    )
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(color = gray(0, alpha = 0.3)) +
  ggplot2::scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.1, 12)) +
  ggplot2::xlab("Age") +
  ggplot2::ylab("Length (mm)") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = get_ages(data_4_model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  ggtitle("Age-to-length conversion for the data_big example data set")
